paper_title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.

Introduction Computer-use agents (CUAs) automate tasks of graphical interfaces by translating natural-language instructions and visual observations into executable actions (Cheng et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024), and are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon automation tasks that can take more than an hour on average (Abhyankar et al., 2026). While frontier proprietary models have been shown to achieve impressive performance leaps (Anthropic, 2026b; OpenAI, 2026), running every single task spanning hundreds of steps with these models raises cost concerns, whereas light open-weight model alone performs poorly on even much simpler tasks (Xie et al., 2024). This creates fundamental trade-off between accuracy and cost efficiency, motivating weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), in which weak agent serves as the primary executor and hands control to strong agent only when needed (Lei and Huang, 2026; Wei et al., 2026). W2SE raises two important questions: (1) When should the weak agent escalate, and (2) who oversees the strong agent after handing over? Existing work on W2SE primarily focuses on the first question, estimating the weak agents failure risk to decide when escalation is needed. Some of them adopt another monitoring agent to verify each step (Wang et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2026), others train an extra monitoring module on the collection of annotated trajectories (Lei and Huang, 2026; Wei et al., 2026). However, the former inevitably adds nontrivial cost to run another heavy agent step-by-step, whereas the latter creates another phase of data annotation and training, hindering direct adoption in real-world applications under varying deployment constraints. While training-free uncertainty estimation-based approaches might avoid the aforementioned bottlenecks (Oh et al., 2026b), prior works still rely on external knowledge base (Liu et al., 2026), another reference model (Oh et al., 2026a), or multiple sampling for each step (Wang et al., 2026) quickly becomes infeasible or impractical in long-horizon tasks in the wild. Besides, escalation alone does not eliminate execution uncertainty, resulting in the second important question in W2SE which is commonly overlooked. That is, even after stronger agent takes control, subsequent actions may deviate from the intended task or fail to achieve the desired outcome. However, monitoring black-box strong agent is challenging because its internal states are inaccessible and verbalized confidence can be unreliable on evolving context of long-horizon task (Han et al., 2024; Kirchhof et al., 2026). To answer both questions, we formulate W2SE as budget-constrained sequential stopping problem, and use the weak agents failure risk as proxy for the expected benefit of escalation. We then propose Latent uncertainty for Escalation And SHadow oversight (LEASH), training-free framework driven by the uncertainty signal in the weak agents hidden states. First, we record its hidden states of prompt and action tokens on small set of held-out tasks and label them with task-level and subgoal-level outcomes to construct representation bank. This representation bank then serves as semantic anchor to score the newly faced prompts and actions during test-time by measuring, under Mahalanobis metric in latent space, how much closer each one lies to past failures than to past successes. LEASH puts this signal on two jobs (Figure 2): For escalation, an initial gate scores uncertainty from the task prompt query, while runtime gate monitors subsequent execution trace. For oversight, after the weak model hands the control to the strong agent, it switches its role from actor to observer that monitors the strong agents trajectory every three steps; when its uncertainty is high, the pending action is rolled back and re-decided once with higher reasoning effort. Importantly, our uncertainty-driven W2SE formulation draws on an easily accessible resource, the weak agents own past experience (Silver and Sutton, 2025), removing reliance on an external dataset or additional training without hosting another expensive agent during runtime, while offering extensibility for recursive self-improvement (Madaan et al., 2023; Schmidhuber, 2007; Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zelikman et al., 2022). 2 LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents Figure 2 Overview of uncertainty-aware weak-to-strong escalation and post-handoff oversight. weak agent goes through the task until its uncertainty scores trigger initial or step-level escalation; otherwise, the weak agent continues. After escalation is triggered, the strong agent retains control while the weak agent changes its role from an actor to shadow observer for continued monitoring. The feedback path from weak observer to strong actor enables uncertainty-triggered reflection and intervention. In short, LEASH unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agents latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on leash afterward. We evaluate LEASH on OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) with four open-weight weak agents and Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a) as the strong agent. At matched escalation rates, LEASH outperforms random escalation by 6.5511.94 points. We further measure how much of the performance gap between the weak agent alone and always-on Opus is recovered by escalation, following the performance-gap metric of (Burns et al., 2023). LEASH recovers 75102% of this gap, against 3769% for random escalation, while costing 6981% as much as always-on Opus. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), LEASH matches always-on Opus (73.7% vs. 72.9% success) at 19% lower cost, whereas random escalation at equal cost scores about 9 points lower (Figure 1). Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formalize weak-to-strong escalation as budget-constrained sequential stopping problem and show that one latent uncertainty signal can drive both escalation and oversight. We propose training-free, scalable uncertainty scoring method that measures how much closer hidden state lies to the weak agents own past failures than to its past successes, and provide theoretical justification for using this score for escalation. We extend this uncertainty signal to weak-to-strong oversight, in which the white-box weak agent monitors the black-box strong agent through its own hidden states. On OSWorld with four open-weight backbones, we show that LEASH outperforms random escalation at matched escalation rates and recovers 75102% of the escalation gap at 6981% of the cost of using always strong agent. 2. Related Work Efficient Computer-Use Agents. Model routing and cascading offer promising way to balance inference cost and performance, as demonstrated by FrugalGPT and RouteLLM (Chen et al., 2023; 3 LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents Dekoninck et al., 2025; Ong et al., 2025). Extending this idea to GUI automation, Adaptive VLM Routing selects models based on action difficulty and confidence (Liu et al., 2026), while StepWise trains lightweight monitors to detect execution stalls and identify milestones for escalation (Wei et al., 2026). Our work instead leverages the backbone agents internal representations to guide both task-level routing and step-level escalation, without training dedicated monitoring network. Weak-to-Strong Paradigms. Weak-to-strong generalization studies how stronger models learn from weaker supervision (Burns et al., 2023; Jung et al., 2025; Medvedev et al., 2025; Somerstep et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025). These works primarily concern training-time transfer of supervision or capabilities from weaker model to stronger one. Here we study the complementary inferencetime setting of weak-to-strong escalation (W2SE), where weak model executes by default and selectively invokes stronger model when additional capability is needed. This shifts the weakstrong relationship from supervision transfer to sequential resource allocation. We derive escalation signals from the agents own past experience without training an additional monitor. Uncertainty Estimation and Agent Monitoring. Uncertainty estimation of agentic systems has emerged as one of the most important problems to monitor and guide agent decisions (Chun et al., 2026; Han et al., 2024; Oh et al., 2026b), while SafeGround and Argus investigate uncertainty estimation for GUI grounding, including calibrated predictions and representation-based methods (Kumar et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Sampling-based uncertainty estimation and risk control have also been studied for question answering (Duan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), but repeated generation can be costly when applied at every step of long-horizon agent trajectory. Meanwhile, another line of work explores weak-to-strong oversight of agent misbehavior and failure monitoring through observable trajectories (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Kale et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026). Rather than focusing on either escalation or oversight alone, we handle both problem in single unified fueled by simple uncertainty estimate. That is, we integrate representation-based uncertainty estimation into the execution workflow, reusing the backbone models hidden states for escalation and extending the same signal to post-handoff oversight of closed-source strong agent. 3. Method We introduce LEASH, training-free uncertainty-driven agentic inference framework for W2SE and post-handoff oversight (Figure 2). By comparing the weak models runtime hidden states with successful and failed reference executions, we estimate uncertainty at task initialization and during execution, which guides both escalation to the strong agent and continued oversight after handoff. We first formulate the problem in Section 3.1 and introduce each component in subsequent sections. 3.1. Problem Formulation Given task query, computer-use agent generates an action conditioned on the query, the screen, and history. We consider lightweight, weak agent, e.g., relatively small open-weight model with accessible hidden states, and large, strong agent, e.g., proprietary black-box frontier model, sharing budget of 𝑇 actions. In addition to these two actor agents, we also host Manager agent (with strong model) who fires at the beginning to decompose the task and subsequently at subgoal boundaries to verify progress, constructing minimal version of multi-agent workflow (Agashe et al., 2025a,b; Koh et al., 2026). Throughout execution, the Manager decomposes the task query into subgoals with screenshot-verifiable completion criteria and decides whether to advance, keep, or revise each subgoal (Appendix C). This decomposition naturally provides finer-grained supervision (Chun 4 LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents and Russakovsky, 2026), allowing execution steps to inherit subgoal-level outcomes rather than relying solely on the final task-level label. Post-Handoff Oversight and Intervention We note that the strong agent can also get stuck in repeated action loops or get lost in multi-turn interactions (Laban et al., 2026). To handle this challenge, we repurpose the weak agent from an actor as Shadow observer of strong agent for continued post-handoff oversight. Task Success and Inference Cost LEASH consistently improves task success over standalone weak-agent execution across all four backbones  (Table 1)  . At closely matched escalation rates, it also outperforms random task escalation by 6.5511.94 percentage points, showing that the training-free uncertainty signal provides useful information for selective weak-to-strong escalation rather than merely increasing access to the strong executor. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a) as the backbone, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success while escalating 64.1% of tasks, compared with 72.90% for always-on Opus (Anthropic, 2026a). Besides, its estimated inference cost is $0.4117 per task, 19.2% lower than the $0.5094 cost of always-on Opus. The benefit also persists at lower escalation rates: LEASH improves Nemotron3 (Deshmukh et al., 2026) from 45.04% to 66.03% success while escalating 43.1% of tasks, and EvoCUA-8B (Xue et al., 2026) from 42.37% to 67.18% while escalating 45.4%. Both methods use Opus 5 as the strong executor and the same cost accounting as LEASH. We see that LEASH outperforms other methods with higher success rate at comparable escalation rate. 4.3. Uncertainty Estimation We compare output probability-based uncertainty estimates with three representation-based alternatives: Euclidean distance to class centroids, kNN over reference representations, and our pooled LDA using covariance-aware Mahalanobis distance. The probability-based baseline considers several uncertainty metrics, including negative log-probability, chosen-token probability, predictive entropy, and nucleus-set size under different aggregation schemes (Gupta et al., 2024), and reports the strongest one in each setting. As shown in Table 3, the effectiveness of each uncertainty estimator (i.e., how well it predicts task or sub-goal failure) varies across both backbones and execution stages. At the initial query-based uncertainty estimation stage, pooled LDA performs best for Nemotron, whereas probability-based baseline is stronger for Qwen3.8-27B. At the runtime step-wise estimation stage, our pooled LDA score achieves the highest AUROC for both backbones, although the overall effectiveness remains moderate. Overall, these results suggest that representation-based uncertainty can provide training-free signal for runtime monitoring, particularly highlighting the effectiveness of our LDA-based estimation, while its effectiveness remains dependent on the backbone and execution stage. Meanwhile, the uncertainty estimator is modular in LEASH, allowing alternative, better uncertainty signals to be substituted without changing the escalation workflow depending on available resources or data (Park et al., 2026a,b). 4.4. Ablation Study Component-wise ablation. As shown in Table 4, the largest gain comes from enabling uncertaintyguided escalation: task success increases from 41.15% with the Manager to 67.94%, at higher inference cost. Adding Shadow monitoring and checkpoint intervention further improves success to 73.66% with only small additional cost, revealing an isolated effectiveness of the post-handoff intervention. We first examine whether uncertainty helps identify which tasks should receive strong-model assistance. Figure 4 varies the escalation budget and compares LEASH with random task-level routing at matched escalation rates. The random baseline is evaluated at the same operating points, shown by the hollow markers; its near-linear trend follows from uniformly allocating fixed fraction of tasks to the strong agent. Across varying escalation rates, LEASH consistently achieves higher task success, indicating that its gains come from selectively allocating strong-model computation to more informative tasks rather than simply increasing strong-model usage. When to escalate. We next examine whether the timing of handoff matters once task is likely to require escalation. We focus on an escalation-prone subset consisting of the tasks most frequently escalated by LEASH and compare LEASH with shuffled-timing baseline. As shown in Figure 5, LEASH achieves 64.6% task success at $0.67 per task, compared with 60.4% at $0.79 under shuffled timing. This 4.2-point improvement, together with 15% lower cost, suggests that effective weak-to-strong escalation depends not only on selecting the right tasks, but also on transferring control at the right point during execution. Theoretical Analysis Section 3 introduced the distance-based uncertainty score in Eq. (3), and Section 4 showed that escalating on that score outperforms random escalation at matched rates. In this section, we now explain the empirical success of our uncertainty-based escalation through simple probabilistic analysis. To keep the analysis simple, we consider single decision per task: each task is either handed to the strong agent before execution begins (𝑡esc = 0) or never handed off (𝑡esc = 𝑇). This isolates the initial gate 𝑔0 of LEASH (Section 3.3), with no runtime escalation afterward. We also assume the budget in Eq. (1) is used exactly, so fixed fraction 𝑝 of tasks is escalated, which is what our quantile thresholds target. Let 𝑧 be the standardized query representation, 𝑌 {Pass, Fail} the outcome if the weak agent completes the task without escalation, and 𝑞w(𝑧) = Pr(𝑌 = Pass 𝑧) and 𝑞s(𝑧) the success probabilities when the weak agent and the strong agent, respectively, completes the task. We analyze 𝑢(𝑧), the population version of our initial score 𝑢𝑞 in Eq. (3), computed with the true class means and covariance instead of their estimates. Proposition 1 (Optimality of LEASHs initial gate at fixed escalation rate). Suppose 𝑧 𝑌 = 𝑦 (𝜇 𝑦, Σ) with shared covariance Σ 0 and distinct means, and both outcomes occur with positive probability. Let the initial gate escalate task when 𝑢(𝑧) exceeds the threshold that escalates fraction 𝑝 of tasks. Among all escalation rules based on 𝑧 with the same rate 𝑝: (i) the gate hands off the largest fraction of the tasks the weak agent would fail, i.e., it maximizes Pr(escalated 𝑌 = Fail); (ii) if the escalation gain Δ(𝑧) = 𝑞s(𝑧) 𝑞w(𝑧) is nondecreasing function of 𝑢(𝑧), and when 𝑞s is constant, the gate also maximizes task success rate. LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents Proof sketch. Under this model, our score equals (up to an additive constant) twice the log-odds that the weak agent fails (Lemma 1 in Appendix A.1), which recalls the classical linear discriminant analysis identity (Fisher, 1936). Escalating the highest-scoring tasks thus escalates the tasks most likely to fail, and NeymanPearson exchange argument (Neyman and Pearson, 1933) shows that no other rule at the same rate catches more failures; (ii) follows by the same argument applied to Δ. Implication. Proposition 1 (i) says that, at any escalation budget, no escalation rule based on the query representation 𝑧 captures more of the weak agents failures than the initial gate of LEASH. For example, random escalation with budget 𝑝 hands off only fraction 𝑝 of these failures, whereas our gate hands off strictly more. Moreover, (ii) shows that our gate spends the strong-agent budget where it pays off most (Jitkrittum et al., 2023), so catching more of the weak agents failures directly turns into higher overall task success. Meanwhile, the analysis covers only the initial gate; analyzing the runtime gate would require an optimal-stopping formulation, which we leave to future work. 6. Conclusion We introduced weak to strong escalation as general inference paradigm for adaptive agent systems, in which inexpensive weak models handle routine execution and stronger models are invoked selectively when additional capability is needed. Under this paradigm, we proposed LEASH, training-free, uncertainty-aware framework that supports initial routing, runtime escalation, and continued posthandoff oversight. Our results suggest that shared latent uncertainty signal can support both selective escalation and post-handoff oversight, providing practical mechanism for dynamically allocating model capability while retaining continued control over strong-agent execution.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our current evaluation is limited to computer-use agents on OSWorld, so the generality of weak-tostrong escalation beyond this domain remains to be validated. In addition, our uncertainty score estimates weak-agent failure risk rather than the expected benefit of escalation; Proposition 1 requires condition that the escalation gain be nondecreasing in the score, which may fail when both weak and strong agents struggle on the same task. Finally, post-handoff Shadow monitoring operates under distribution shift from weak-agent trajectories, and its intervention effect is not causally isolated in our current evaluation. 12 LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents

Reference Banks and Threshold Calibration Reference banks. For each backbone, we construct small held-out set of Manager-guided trajectories collected with escalation disabled and disjoint from the evaluation tasks. From this set, we construct the query and action representation banks: initial representations are labeled by tasklevel outcomes, while runtime representations inherit the outcomes of their corresponding subgoal segments. Held-out scoring. We use the same held-out reference set for both representation-bank construction and threshold calibration. Specifically, we perform task-grouped 10-fold cross-validation, keeping all steps from the same task in one fold. For each fold, an uncertainty estimator is fitted on the other nine folds and used only to score the held-out fold, yielding one out-of-fold score for every reference task. The fold-specific estimators are used only for calibration and are discarded afterwards. We then set the escalation thresholds as empirical quantiles of these out-of-fold scores. After calibration, we fit one final estimator per uncertainty channel on all tasks in the same reference set, keep the calibrated thresholds fixed, and use these final estimators to score the evaluation tasks. No evaluation data are used for either estimator fitting or threshold calibration. Targets and thresholds. All four backbones use the same targets, 𝑝𝑞 = 0.25 and 𝑝esc = 0.50, so that 𝑝𝑎 = ( 𝑝esc 𝑝𝑞)/(1 𝑝𝑞) = 1/3. The thresholds 𝜏𝑞 and 𝜏𝑎 are exact order statistics of the held-out scores in Eq. (4). Because the reference set is finite, the achievable rates are discrete, with resolution of one reference task. A.4. Post-Handoff Oversight Probe schedule and context. Shadow probes run at the first strong-agent step after handoff and at every third step thereafter. At every strong-agent step, including steps without probe, the executed action is appended to the weak models history in that models own action format, so that each probe conditions on the actual trajectory rather than on the pre-handoff context. probe calls the weak agents own action-generation routine, with its usual system prompt, tool schema, and image history, and does not invoke the Manager. The candidate action is logged for analysis but never executed or shown to the strong agent. Shadow threshold. 𝜏sh is the 90th percentile of the pooled per-step runtime scores over the 99-task reference pool, computed separately for each backbone. It is derived directly from the reference pool rather than from the escalation thresholds. For EvoCUA-8B, the in-sample value (+1.7309) is close to the corresponding out-of-fold value (+1.7106). Checkpoint budget. At most six checkpoints can fire in an episode. In addition, once two checkpoints have changed the strong agents action, further firings are suppressed; checkpoints that leave the action unchanged do not count toward this second limit. Because probes occur every three steps, consecutive checkpoints are at least three steps apart. Checkpoint mechanics. When checkpoint fires, the strong agents conversation is truncated to its length at the start of the current step, which removes the pending action; the neutral checkpoint message in Figure 7 is appended; and the strong agent re-decides the step with raised reasoningeffort setting. The weak models candidate action is deliberately excluded from the checkpoint message, so the strong agent is never steered toward specific action proposed by the weaker model. 20 LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents B. Additional Experimental Results B.1. Experimental Details Evaluation setting. We evaluate on OSWorld with screenshot observations and shared budget of 50 actions per task. The lightweight backbones are EvoCUA-8B (Xue et al., 2026), Qwen3.535B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026a), Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni (30B-A3B) (Deshmukh et al., 2026), and Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026a) serves as both the Manager and strong executor, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025) is an additional always-on reference. The always-on references run the strong model alone, without the Manager, so they measure strongmodel capability without the Manager or escalation framework. Configurations and evaluation sets. Manager adds subgoal planning and verification; Escalation further enables initial and runtime handoff; and LEASH additionally enables post-handoff Shadow monitoring and corresponding intervention. These configurations are cumulative. Shared results below follow Tables 1 and 4. The evaluation task pool contains 262 tasks. Reference banks and calibration. We use held-out reference set that is disjoint from the 262 evaluation tasks. We obtain task-grouped 10-fold out-of-fold scores, keeping all observations from task in one fold; preprocessing and estimator fitting use only the training folds. Initial scores use final task outcomes and runtime scores use Manager-assigned subgoal outcomes. Thresholds are order statistics of the held-out scores targeting 25% initial and 50% overall escalation frequency, with runtime calibration based on per-task maximum scores. Refitting slightly changes the score scale, and differences between the reference and evaluation sets can further affect the realized escalation rate; hence the observed rates (4364%) need not exactly match the calibration targets. Post-handoff execution. After handoff, Shadow probes query the lightweight model every three strong-agent steps. Probe actions are not executed; their hidden representations provide the monitoring scores. Higher scores indicate greater uncertainty and can trigger an intervention that asks the strong agent to reassess its current strategy while retaining control. Cost estimation. We estimate inference cost from recorded token usage using OpenRouter reference prices, accounting for cached tokens where applicable. Total cost includes lightweight-agent, Manager, strong-executor, and monitoring calls. For locally served models, we report reference inference-cost estimates rather than measured hardware costs.
